> I still think so. bswap gives low level swapping but doesn’t on its own necessarily give direct encoding/decoding or automatic integration in PackedByteArray. These `encode_x_be` methods just serve as complimentary BE implementations for the current `encode_x` methods available, and make the intention much clearer and less verbose

The main issue this addresses is that the alternative to decode the first four bytes of data in BE from a PackedByteArray would be something along the lines of:
```
array.bswap32().decode_u32()
```
And it gets worse if you wanted it to be non-destructive:
```
array.slice(0, 4).bswap32().decode_u32()
```
So the new methods help make this much more readable and intuitive: 
```
array.decode_u32_be()
```
Throughout the development of 4.5 and forward I've seen pushes towards more explicit distinctions between big endian and little endian operations (FileAccess in particular), so this would just be an extension of that.

@cruglet
Have you seen the PR for bswap? 
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/105145

You've mentioned bswap provides low level swapping, I'm not entirely sure what you mean by this, as the PR shows that these methods were specifically introduced for working with big endian data.

Your changes certainly provide an alternative way to work with big endian data, you present a strong case for how it's more concise than bswap. This comes at the cost of introducing many more methods, and making bswap mostly redundant.

If you still believe it's best to merge this PR, I think it needs a compelling case that demonstrates a wide-enough need that outweighs the inconvenience of using bswap.

> See above

I do not see any mentions of real world use cases.

This might be a bit cleaner than using `bswap` (which itself only exist to swap large chunks of data without performance impact, for something `slice(0, 4).bswap32()` it can be done by manually swapping bytes), but if it's used only for a few obscure file formats, it probably is not worth adding core functions.

> Have you seen the PR for bswap?
> https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/105145
> You've mentioned bswap provides low level swapping, I'm not entirely sure what you mean by this, as the PR shows that these methods were specifically introduced for working with big endian data. 

The PR "partially adressess" the problem. `bswap` is a low-level utility for swapping byte order, but it doesn’t change the fact that the encode_x and decode_x methods operate in little endian by default. The main issue with `bswap` in this case is that it blindly swaps bytes in fixed-width chunks without any awareness of the semantic structure of the data.

> Your changes certainly provide an alternative way to work with big endian data, you present a strong case for how it's more concise than bswap. This comes at the cost of introducing many more methods, and making bswap mostly redundant.
>
> If you still believe it's best to merge this PR, I think it needs a compelling case that demonstrates a wide-enough need that outweighs the inconvenience of using bswap.

I would also like to echo some points brought up in the related issue linked to the bswap PR (cc @YuriSizov):
- Mutating data just to work around the lack of endianness control in encode_x/decode_x isn’t ideal.
- Currently, bswap doesn’t really offer more than what could be done with a reverse and a copy of the section you want to read/write, except maybe for very large homogeneous data chunks. This very quickly breaks down when working with buffers that have multiple different data types in one stream, let alone if some of that mixed data isn't necessarily BE.
- One offered compromise was to add the flag to all encode_* and decode_* methods directly (which was originally done in my PR), or to introduce new methods for BE. I shifted to the latter in this case.


> > See above
> 
> I do not see any mentions of real world use cases.
> 
> This might be a bit cleaner than using `bswap` (which itself only exist to swap large chunks of data without performance impact, for something `slice(0, 4).bswap32()` it can be done by manually swapping bytes), but if it's used only for a few obscure file formats, it probably is not worth adding core functions.

I get where this is coming from, but I feel as though this conflates frequency of use in specific cases with API completeness and correctness. Claiming this is bloat overlooks that `bswap` and BE encode/decode serve fundamentally different purposes. In fact, the very existence of a dedicated `bswap` method acknowledges that working with different endianness types is important enough to warrant core support. This BE encode/decode extension is simply a complementary & safe way to fill that gap, not necessarily redundant or niche.

> I do not see any mentions of real world use cases.

With all due respect, I didn't see any real world cases in #105145 either. It vaguely referenced the proposal, which it supposedly partially addressed, but didn't explain how or why it was the best option to address said proposal (and nobody in the proposal suggested this approach).

I'm honestly a bit confused by the lack of any discussion on #105145 regarding its merits and value, as it seemingly comes out of nowhere and its relation to the proposal is very much tangential. Maybe the discussion happened off this platform, but it's not referenced anywhere as far as I can tell.

So I don't see why an increased level of scrutiny is necessary for this PR which is directly addressing the proposal and the real world cases described in it.

-----

Now, I've already [offered my take](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/9586#issuecomment-2796392216) on why the solution proposed by #105145 is not satisfactory, and @cruglet helpfully repeated some of my points here, above. I'll only add that I don't think it's fair to call a mainstream and widespread file format like MIDI, for example, an obscure one. It's old, yes. It's pretty much stuck in place because of that too. But it's, like, standard, and its use in gaming software is actually very common.

Can it be supported without additional engine changes? [Yeah](https://github.com/YuriSizov/boscaceoil-blue/blob/main/io/MidiExporter.gd), [sure](https://github.com/YuriSizov/boscaceoil-blue/blob/main/utils/ByteArrayUtil.gd). The proposal asks for convenience tools, and `bswap` doesn't introduce any additional convenience for the examples that I can see. You don't create MIDI in giant chunks that can be bswapped. You write a lot of small sequences though, and bswapping them doesn't make things clearer or easier to implement whatsoever.

> it blindly swaps bytes in fixed-width chunks without any awareness of the semantic structure of the data

This is how you swap endianess! All of the new methods can be implemented in terms of bswap, as reviewers have indicated, the code even compiles down to a single bswap instruction in some cases.

The existing bswap methods have an offset and count, let's say you want to decode a big endian uint32:
```
bswap32(offset, 1) 
decode_u32(offset) 
bswap32(offset, 1) // optional, restore the original data 
```

An additional section in the PackedByteArray documentation for dealing with big endian data could help to resolve any confusion? 

@YuriSizov, is it your position, that if this PR is merged, that  bswap should be deprecated? With a recommendation to use the appropriate encoding methods instead?

It just seems odd to introduce 3 methods for handling big endian data in one release only to introduce 18 new methods (that's a lot) in the next release that are functionally equivalent to calling up to three existing methods in sequence.

I would not oppose replacing `bswap*` with this, but it's already in 4.5, we can't simply remove it without breaking compatibly, so it's simply too late to do this. And adding 18 new methods feels a bit excessive to have a bit shorter and cleaner code.

Also, `decode_*_be` methods might be confusing for new users, endianess is a pretty obscure concept and most game developers never have to deal with it.

> > it blindly swaps bytes in fixed-width chunks without any awareness of the semantic structure of the data
> 
> This is how you swap endianess! All of the new methods can be implemented in terms of bswap, as reviewers have indicated, the code even compiles down to a single bswap instruction in some cases.
> 
> The existing bswap methods have an offset and count, let's say you want to decode a big endian uint32:
> 
> ```
> bswap32(offset, 1) 
> decode_u32(offset) 
> bswap32(offset, 1) // optional, restore the original data 
> ```

This approach quickly becomes unnecessarily verbose and cumbersome rather quickly. Needing to write three lines of code just to read a single big-endian integer is excessive for something that should be a one-liner.

Endianness handling is a fundamental operation in data parsing, serialization, and networking code (or MIDI, as mentioned by @YuriSizov). Forcing developers to manually juggle byte swaps before and after a read is not only tedious but also error-prone, harder to read, and clutters otherwise simple logic. There is simply no reason for users to repeatedly spell out this boilerplate when the library could provide a clearer, self-explanatory API for these type of operations.

> It just seems odd to introduce 3 methods for handling big endian data in one release only to introduce 18 new methods (that's a lot) in the next release that are functionally equivalent to calling up to three existing methods in sequence.

The “3 existing methods” solution is not functionally equivalent in any meaningful sense. It’s a manual, multi-step workaround that temporarily mutates what is in memory to achieve what should be a one-step read. 

Ideally, a BE flag would be set similar to FileAccess so that the very same encoding/decoding methods can be used, but that isn't really possible with the current implementation. 

Likewise, adding an optional endian parameter to the currently existing methods would break API compatibility, which is exactly why these additional methods were introduced (as you yourself suggested earlier @bruvzg). At the time, this approach was encouraged and the implementation was approved, so I'm confused as to why all of a sudden it's a major problem now.

> Also, decode_*_be methods might be confusing for new users, endianess is a pretty obscure concept and most game developers never have to deal with it.

This seems to actually reinforce why explicit BE methods are valuable. Endianness _is_ a more obscure concept, but that doesn’t mean the API should hide it or force users to perform low-level byte swaps manually. In fact, the complexity should be abstracted and explained/reflected in the documentation, not ignored.

And if this were not the case, working with `PackedByteArray`s already implies that you are dealing with raw binary data. In that context, developers are either likely already aware of endianness, or at the very least capable of understanding it with minimal guidance. Explicit BE methods simply make the intent obvious, safe, and easier to use correctly, while the documentation can provide any additional explanation for those new to the concept.

Don't get me wrong; I'm not saying that adding all of these methods is _definitively_ the best option, but the current workarounds in order to deal with BE data are either way too verbose, confusing, or a combination of the two for operations that are so simple.

If you are worried about lines of code and overhead, perhaps we should consider adding bswap functions to @GlobalScope?

```gdscript
int bswap16(x: int)
int bswap32(x: int)
int bswap64(x: int)

# returns x with the underlying byte order swapped, for the least N significant bits, useful
# for converting to big endian values from little endian values and vice versa.

bswap32(decode_u32(offset)) # decodes a big endian uint32 at offset
```
EDIT (removed floats): on further thought, I don't think this approach would work for floats, they would need to be loaded as an integer in this way, with a mechanism to bitcast them back to the appropriate float.

As @bruvzg has mentioned, I don't think anybody is trying to argue here that bswap methods are more intuitive, but it's also a reality that big-endian data is primarily a special case concern today. This is why there is some hesitation about adding 18 new methods and an explicit decision point (particularly, by newcomers who are just trying to serialize some game data) about which one to use.

Everyone seems to agree that adding a toggle (that defaults to little-endian) to the PackedByteArray (or its methods) is another good solution and this may be possible in the future if builtin methods get compatibility hashes for GDExtension, or the underlying data structure is changed. Merging this now would realistically shut down a potentially better option for dealing with big-endian data until something like Godot 5.

> If you are worried about lines of code and overhead, perhaps we should consider adding bswap functions to @globalscope?
> 
> ```gdscript
> int bswap16(x: int)
> int bswap32(x: int)
> int bswap64(x: int)
> 
> # returns x with the underlying byte order swapped, for the least N significant bits, useful
> # for converting to big endian values from little endian values and vice versa.
> # Supported types: int, float
> 
> bswap32(decode_u32(offset)) # decodes a big endian uint32 at offset

This is definitely an improvement and I feel like we're approaching a good compromise!

My one and only issue with this is that I'm unsure on whether its a good idea to rely on the "possibility" of Godot 5 being able to implement the functionality aforementioned.

One alternative I would perhaps propose is creating some universal class that handles all kinds of buffers, and then have that be able to handle all complex binary logic, but I'm unsure as to whether or not that would be too much in conjunction with PackedByteArray and FileAccess.
```gdscript
var buffer: BinaryBuffer = BinaryBuffer.from_file("/path/to/file.bin")
```
or maybe something like:
``` gdscript
var buffer: BinaryBuffer = byte_array.to_buffer()
```
And then you can work with it like this:
```gdscript
buffer.big_endian = true
buffer.write_u32(112)
buffer.seek(0x50)
int flag = buffer.read_u16()
int other_flag = buffer.read_bits(3)
buffer.seek_to_end()
buffer.write_u8(flag)
buffer.to_file("/path/to/file2.bin")
```
We can also implement both BE and LE struct unpacking (similar to python), which is mostly the issue that prompted this PR for me:
(Its also possible that this can also be implemented into PackedByteArray as well, with some considerations)
```gdscript
var struct_data: Array[int] = buffer.unpack(">HHxBBxLLLLxB")
```
Perhaps something like that could be useful, if this sounds like a good idea I can make a proposal for it. Otherwise, I'd like to hear more about what other paths we could take if the BE specific methods just absolutely can't be added.

That seems like an option, FileAccess already looks a lot like a BinaryBuffer (except tied to a particular file) and one of the annoying things about PackedByteArrays is tracking offsets.

Would it be possible to introduce something like a virtual BinaryBuffer/BinaryAccess class that FileAccess simply inherits its existing data-manipulation methods from? Would this be backwards compatible (enough)? Then you could have something like FileAccess and MemoryAccess and GDExtensions could provide their own BinaryBuffer/BinaryAccess implementations too, ie. exposing runtime-specific memory directly (ie. without copying it into a PackedByteArray).

I'm certainly happy to help if needed.

As far as I know the current workaround is any time we need to do an endian swap we use https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_streampeerbuffer.html The super class has an endian method. It's not very neat, but it's also relatively simple to use. TL;DR it's a thing in operating system research since the 1970s where SOCKETS are not files. There's been some work in Plan9 to unify everything to be files, but those operating systems are not in overwhelmingly widespread use.

I hope its possible, and I really like the sound of this. Perhaps this way we could even allow to specifiy a read/write-only buffer just like FileAccess, for safety.
```gdscript
var buf = BinaryAccess.from_bytes(byte_array, BinaryAccess.READ)
```
I would say FileAccess to some degree is more feature-complete for handling serial binary buffers than PackedByteArray so making a universal superclass for it to inherit from makes sense, I just hope its feasable.

This feels like a much better way to do it. Cleaner and can be used with anything, not just `PackedByteArray`.
